newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COFFEE -- ACPC meeting to push spotlight on Brazil.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE -- ACPC meeting to push spotlight on Brazil.

text.p: Rio de Janeiro will next week become the focus of the world coffee market, with the city acting as the venue for an emergency council of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) on January 23.

The council follows a three-day seminar looking at important changes in the Brazilian coffee sector which in turn follows the official installation of one of these changes, the Conselho Deliberativo da Politica Cafeeira or CDPC, on January 17.

"Coffee is the flavour of the moment in Brazil," said Maurico Assis, head of the primary commodities department at the Industry and Commerce Ministry after a meeting today with exporters in Rio de Janeiro.

The CDPC is the new private and public sector body which in future is to decide on Brazilian coffee policy. But at today's meeting, Assis made quite clear that foreign policy was still the prerogative of the government.
This is demonstrated by the fact there will only be a signing ceremony for the CDPC on January 17 in Brasilia.
There are no plans for an actual meeting of the CDPC in preparation for next week's ACPC council, Assis said.

The ACPC council is expected to address the issue of whether there is a need to cut exports by member countries in the January to June period which, under the current ACPC plan, should not exceed 26.28 million 60-kg bags.
Already African nations led by the Ivory Coast and with the backing of Colombia have called for exports to be reduced by around a further 2.5 million bags.
Analysts expect a cut to be agreed but for robusta coffee shipments, leaving arabica coffee untouched.
Exporters discussed the situation with Assis this morning and will also meet with government officials during the coffee seminar, probably on January 22, Assis said.

Any decision on a change in ACPC policy would be taken by the government but Assis declined to say what was the government's current position in relation to further possible cuts, preferring to wait for the meeting itself.
"You have to be flexible," was his only comment.
Under the current scheme, Brazil should ship no more than six million bags in the January to June period after a limit of nine million bags in July to December.
According to figures issued by the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Federation (Febec) which are based on bills of lading, actual exports in the last six months were 8.98 million bags.
The government, working with requests for shipment authorisations, has a figure of 9.07 million bags but the tiny surplus does not represent any cause for concern, Assis said.

Within Brazil, there is concern unless the government raises the size of its monthly sales considerably, there will not be enough coffee available to meet the six million bag limit as producers hold on to what they have in expectations of a smaller crop in 1997/98.
Hence exporters again at today's meeting called for higher auctions and also more sales of coffee of adequate qualities to meet the needs of exporters, said Oswaldo Aranha, FEBEC president.
